name: Board Density Estimator
blurb: density class and routing difficulty from part count and area
intro: How full the board is and whether it will route: pin density sets the density class, and the wiring the netlist needs (links × average link length) is compared with what the routing layers can hold at your track and space. The demand/capacity method follows Coombs' Printed Circuits Handbook; the class limits and the link-length factor are rules of thumb.

inputs.label: Total pin count
inputs.help: Sum of pads that connect to nets (from the netlist or BOM).

inputs.label: Average pins per net
inputs.help: 2-3 for most boards; higher with many buses or big ground nets counted.

examples.title: Compact wearable, 35 × 25 mm, both sides, 4 routing layers

usage: Give board width and height in mm, parts, total pins, average courtyard in mm², the number of signal routing layers, track and clearance in mm, and average pins per net. It returns pin density (pins/in² and pins/cm²), the density class, placement fill in %, wiring demand and capacity in metres, the demand/capacity ratio as a routing difficulty, and the routing layers needed for 50 % utilisation. Use it early to pick layer count and board size, or to judge an existing layout.
sources: C. F. Coombs, Printed Circuits Handbook, 7th ed., McGraw-Hill: wiring demand vs wiring capacity (density evaluation)
H. Holden, The HDI Handbook, ch. 2 (density and wiring formulas)
Rule of thumb: pin-density classes, link length 2.25·√(area/part), 50 % channel usability
